'''John Greaves''' (1602 – 8 October 1652) was an [[England|English]] [[mathematician]], [[astronomer]] and [[antiquarian]].

== Education ==
Educated at [[Balliol College, Oxford]], he was elected a Fellow of [[Merton College]] in 1624. He studied Persian and Arabic, acquired a number of old books and manuscripts for archbishop [[William Laud]] (some still in [[Merton College Library]]), and wrote a treatise (in Latin) on the [[Persian language]]. He travelled in [[Italy]] and the [[Levant]] from 1636 to 1640 and made a survey of the [[Great Pyramid of Giza]].

He was [[Gresham Professor of Geometry]] at [[Gresham College, London]], and [[Savilian professor of astronomy]] at [[Oxford University]],{{sfn|Chisholm|1911|p=422}} and collected [[astrolabes]] and astronomical measuring devices (now in the [[Museum of the History of Science]], Oxford). He was particularly interested in the study of weights and measures, and wrote a treatise on the Roman [[foot (unit)|foot]] and [[denarius]], and was a keen [[numismatist (specialist)|numismatist]]. In 1645 he attempted a reform of the [[Julian calendar]], which was not adopted.

During the [[English Civil War]] he supported [[Charles I of England|Charles I]], who stayed at Merton College while in [[Oxford]], but lost his academic positions at Oxford in 1647 through the animosity of [[Nathaniel Brent]], Warden of Merton College and a [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian]].

==Biography==
===Early life===
He was born in [[Colemore]], near [[Old Alresford|Alresford]], [[Hampshire]]. He was the eldest son of John Greaves, rector of [[Colemore]], and Sarah Greaves.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Shalev
 |first=Zur
 |year=2005
 |title=The travel notebooks of John Greaves
 |journal=Intersections: Yearbook for Early Modern Studies
 |volume=5
 |pages=77–102
 |place=Leiden
 |publisher=Koninklijke Brill NV.
 |url=https://goslide.org/Documents/the-travel-notebooks-of-john-greaves-in-the-republic-of-letters-and-the-levant-intersections-5-2005-edited-by-a-hamilton-m-van-den-boogert-b-westerweel-leiden-brill-2005-pp-77-102|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180816194523/https://goslide.org/Documents/the-travel-notebooks-of-john-greaves-in-the-republic-of-letters-and-the-levant-intersections-5-2005-edited-by-a-hamilton-m-van-den-boogert-b-westerweel-leiden-brill-2005-pp-77-102
 |archive-date=16 August 2018
 |url-status=dead
 }}</ref> His brothers were [[Nicholas Greaves]], [[Thomas Greaves (orientalist)|Thomas Greaves]] and Sir [[Edward Greaves (physician)|Edward Greaves]], physician to [[Charles II of England|Charles II]].

[[File:William Laud.jpg|thumb|[[William Laud]], patron of Merton College]]
His father ran a school for sons of the neighbouring gentry, where Greaves began his education.<ref>[[Macquorn Rankine]], W. J. in [https://archive.org/stream/imperialdictiona02eadi#page/712/mode/2up ''Imperial Dictionary of Universal Biography''] Vol II, p.713 London: William Mackenzie</ref> Aged 15, he went to [[Balliol College, Oxford]] between 1617&ndash;1621, gaining a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] degree. In 1624 he was the first of five newly elected Fellows of [[Merton College]], becoming [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)|M.A.]] in 1628.<ref name=Birch>{{cite book |title=Miscellaneous works of Mr. John Greaves |last=Birch |first=Thomas |year=1737 |publisher=J. Brindley and C. Corbett |location=London |page=i–lxxii |url=https://archive.org/details/miscellaneouswo13unkngoog}}</ref> He began to study astronomy and oriental languages, and especially the works of the ancient eastern astronomers. In 1630 Greaves was chosen [[Gresham Professor of Geometry]] at [[Gresham College, London]]. Through his predecessor, [[Peter Turner (mathematician)|Peter Turner]], he later met [[Archbishop of Canterbury|archbishop]] [[William Laud]], the [[List of Chancellors of the University of Oxford|chancellor of Oxford University]] and Visitor (patron) of Merton College. Laud was keen to make English editions of Greek and Arabic authors, and Greaves' later travels abroad involved collecting manuscripts and books for presentation to his new patron.

===Travels in Italy===
[[File:Rzym Fontanna Czterech Rzek.jpg|thumb|The Obelisk of Domitian, now restored in the [[Piazza Navona]] ]]

Greaves enrolled at [[University of Leyden]] in 1633, where he became friends with [[Jacob Golius]], professor of Arabic at Leyden. He enrolled at the [[University of Padua]] in 1635 along with [[George Ent]], meeting the Dane [[Johan Rode]] (John Rhodius), an expert on ancient weights and measures, who also made a commentary on [[Celsus]]. A brief return to England was followed by a second European journey; in 1636 he sailed via [[Livorno]] (Leghorn) to Rome, dining with Ent on 5 October at the [[English College, Rome]]; he also met [[William Harvey]], who was entertained at the college on the 12th, [[Gasparo Berti]], [[Lucas Holstenius]] and [[Athanasius Kircher]].

Probably in the same month he met and consulted with the [[Thomas Howard, 21st Earl of Arundel|Earl of Arundel]]'s art-collecting agent, William Petty (who dined at the college on 14 October), on the Earl's attempted acquisition of the Obelisk of Domitian, then still lying broken in the [[Circus of Maxentius]]. Though "now it is broken into 5 stones", he measured these and including a sketch of the obelisk as hypothetically repaired in his almanac-notebook (Bodleian Library Savile MS 49,1). Though Arundel paid a 60 crown deposit for the obelisk, [[pope Urban VIII]] vetoed its export and it was erected by his successor [[Pope Innocent X|Innocent X]] above [[Bernini]]'s ''Fountain of the Four Rivers'' in the [[Piazza Navona]].<ref>[[Edward Chaney]], "Roma Britannica and the Cultural Memory of Egypt: Lord Arundel and the Obelisk of Domitian", in ''Roma Britannica: Art Patronage and Cultural Exchange in Eighteenth-Century Rome'', eds. D. Marshall, K. Wolfe and S. Russell, British School at Rome, 2011, pp. 147–70, fig. 11.11.</ref>

Greaves toured the [[Catacombs]] and made drawings of the [[Pantheon, Rome|Pantheon]] and [[Pyramid of Cestius]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}} During his stay in Rome he instituted inquiries into the ancient [[weights and measures]]{{sfn|Chisholm|1911|p=422}} that are among the early classics of [[metrology]].

===Travels in the Levant===
[[File:Kheops-Pyramid.jpg|thumb|The Great Pyramid of Khufu, surveyed by Greaves in around 1639]]
In 1637 he made a journey to the [[Levant]], one intention being to fix the [[latitude]] of [[Alexandria]] where [[Ptolemy]] had made his astronomical observations. He sailed from England to Livorno in the company of [[Edward Pococke]]; after a brief visit to Rome, he arrived in [[Istanbul]] (Constantinople) around April 1638. There he made the acquaintance of the English ambassador [[Peter Wyche (ambassador)|Sir Peter Wyche]]. He procured various manuscripts there, including a copy of [[Ptolemy]]'s [[Almagest]] ("the fairest work I ever saw").<ref>Greaves, John (1647); ''A Discourse on the Roman Foot and Denarius'' London: Wm Lee. p.47</ref> Greaves ended up owning two copies of the Almagest. He was going to have visited the many monastic libraries at [[Mount Athos]], in order to make a catalogue of their MSS and unprinted books. Athos was normally open only to members of the Orthodox church, but thanks to a special dispensation from the [[Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople|Patriarch of Constantinople]] [[Cyril Lucaris]], Greaves would have had access; but the execution of the patriarch by strangulation in June 1638 for treason against Sultan [[Murad IV]] prevented his journey.<ref name="Birch"/>

Instead, Greaves continued on to Alexandria, where he collected a number of [[Arabic language|Arabic]], [[Persian language|Persian]] and [[Greek language|Greek]] manuscripts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Printonly/Greaves_John.html|title=Greaves_John (print-only)|website=www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk|access-date=2017-11-23}}</ref> He was an inveterate note-taker, making countless observations in notebooks and on blank pages of other books he bought; he also visited Cairo twice, and made a more accurate survey of the [[Egyptian pyramids|pyramids of Egypt]] than any traveller who had preceded him.{{sfn|Chisholm|1911|p=422}} He returned to England in 1640.

===Calendar reform===
On the death of [[John Bainbridge (astronomer)|John Bainbridge]] in 1643, Greaves was appointed as [[Savilian professor of astronomy]] and senior reader of the [[Thomas Linacre|Linacre]] lecture at Oxford,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Honours/Savilian.html|title=Savilian Chairs|website=www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk|access-date=2017-11-23}}</ref> but he was deprived of his Gresham professorship for having neglected its duties.{{sfn|Chisholm|1911|p=422}} In 1645 he essayed a reformation of the [[Julian calendar]]; but although his plan of omitting the [[bissextile day]] (29 February) for the next 40 years was approved by the king, the matter was dropped owing to the [[English Civil War|turbulent times]].{{citation needed|date=October 2023}} The [[Gregorian calendar]] was not adopted in Britain until 1752.

===Ejection from Oxford===
[[File:Merton college, front quadrangle 01.JPG|thumb|The front [[quadrangle (architecture)|quadrangle]] of [[Merton College, Oxford|Merton College]] ]]

In 1642 Greaves had been elected subwarden of Merton College. Merton was the only Oxford college to [[Merton College#Parliamentarian sympathies in the Civil War|side with the Parliamentarians]] in the [[English Civil War]], through an earlier dispute in 1638 between [[Nathaniel Brent]], the Warden of Merton, and Greaves' patron [[William Laud]]. Brent had been a witness for the prosecution at Laud's 1644 trial. After Laud was executed on 10 January 1645, Greaves drew up a petition for Brent's removal from office; Brent was deposed by Charles I on 27 January.

However, in 1647 a [[Parliamentary visitation of the University of Oxford|Parliamentary commission (or visitation)]] was set up "for the correction of offences, abuses, and disorders" in the University of Oxford. Nathaniel Brent was the president of the visitors.<ref name = DNB>[[:s:Page:Dictionary of National Biography volume 06.djvu/274|''Dictionary of National Biography'', article on Brent, Sir Nathaniel]], pp. 262–4</ref> After [[Thomas Fairfax]] had captured Oxford for the Parliamentarians in 1648 and Brent had returned from London, Greaves was accused of sequestrating the college's plate and funds for [[Charles I of England|king Charles]].<ref name=Ward>[[John Ward (academic)|Ward, John]] (1740). [https://books.google.com/books?id=jp5bAAAAQAAJ ''The Lives of the Professors of Gresham College, to which is prefixed the Life of the Founder, Sir Thomas Gresham''], pp. 144–146 London: John Moore. Google Books full view, retrieved 10 May 2011</ref> Despite a deposition from his brother [[Thomas Greaves (orientalist)|Thomas]], Greaves had lost both his Merton fellowship and his Savilian chair by 9 November 1648. Many of his books and MSS disappeared after his rooms were rifled by soldiers, although his friend [[John Selden]] managed to recover some of them.  However, Greaves was not actually deprived of the professorship until August 1649.{{sfn|Twells|1816|p=123}}

He was succeeded as [[Savilian Professor of Astronomy]] in that year by [[Seth Ward (bishop of Salisbury)|Seth Ward]], who ensured that Greaves was paid the arrears (£500) of his salary; Greaves was unlikely to have got his money, since the Savilian professors were paid from the income of lands held in Kent and Essex, which were under control of Parliament (rather than the king). Ward also gave over a considerable amount of his own salary to Greaves.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Life of Seth Ward, Lord Bishop of Salisbury |last=Pope |first=Walter |year=1697 |publisher=Wm. Keeblewhite |location=London |pages=18–21 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aU46AAAAcAAJ}}</ref>

===Later life and death===
But Greaves' private fortune more than sufficed for all his wants until his death;{{sfn|Chisholm|1911|p=422}} he retired to London, married and occupied his leisure writing and editing books and manuscripts. He died in London aged 50, and was buried in the church of [[St Benet Sherehog]], which was destroyed during the [[Great Fire of London]].<ref name=Ward/>

His brother [[Nicholas Greaves]] was his executor.<ref>[http://www.ebooksread.com/authors-eng/church-of-england-province-of-canterbury-preroga/abstracts-of-probate-acts-in-the-prerogative-court-of-canterbury-volume-6-ruh/page-9-abstracts-of-probate-acts-in-the-prerogative-court-of-canterbury-volume-6-ruh.shtml ''Abstracts of probate acts in the Prerogative court of Canterbury'' (Volume 6)]. Will proved 19th? October 1652.</ref> He left his cabinet containing his coin collection to [[Sir John Marsham, 1st Baronet|Sir John Marsham]], and his astronomical instruments to the university, for the use of the Savilian professors.{{sfn|Smith|1707|p=34}} Two of his astrolabes (inscribed by his brother Nicholas) are in the [[Museum of the History of Science]], Oxford. (see External links)

==Greaves' astronomical instruments==
[[File:Edward Pococke.jpg|thumb|Bust of Edward Pococke in [[Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford]] ]]
Greaves had entrusted his will to his friend and fellow-traveller in the Levant, the scholar of Arabic [[Edward Pococke]]. The will had originally stipulated that Greaves' collection of astronomical instruments ([[astrolabes]], [[quadrant (instrument)|quadrant]]s, [[telescopes]] etc.) was to be left to [[University of Oxford|Oxford university]]. But by 1649 Greaves (who was staying at [[Sir John Marsham]]'s house in [[Rochester, Kent]]) had become increasingly exasperated with the academic situation at Oxford since the civil war. He wrote to Pococke asking to him to send the will to blot out his gift of his instruments to the university (which had cost him more than a hundred pounds), because he "so far despaired of any future encouragement to learning and ingenuity in Oxford."  Greaves repeated his request a few months later, asking Pococke to open the will and strike the words out himself.{{sfn|Twells|1816|p=124}} Pococke seems to have eventually complied with Greaves' wishes, since after Greaves' death in 1652 his executor and brother [[Nicholas Greaves]] kept hold of his late brother's collection.

However, when the [[Commonwealth of England|Commonwealth]] ended with the resignation of [[Richard Cromwell]] in 1659, Nicholas Greaves (in accordance with his late brother's original intent) presented the instruments - suitably inscribed - for the use of the [[Savilian Professor of Astronomy|Savilian Professors of Astronomy]]. They were kept in the professor's room at the top of the Eastern Tower of the [[Oxford Schools]], now the [[Bodleian Library]]. A list of them appears in the 1697 Catalogue' of Bodleian manuscripts<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Sheldonian Theatre| title = Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum Angliæ et Hiberniæ in unum collecti, cum indice alphabetico| location = Oxford| date = 1697 |url=https://onb.digital/result/107C74A1 |language=la |volume=1 |page=302}}, cited in {{harvnb|Smith|1707|p=34}}</ref> In 1710 the collection was held in the Museum Savilianum.{{sfn|Smith|1707|p=34}}

The instruments had disappeared by the 1920s when [[R. T. Gunther]], the first curator of the Oxford [[Museum of the History of Science]], made inquiries into their whereabouts. Gunther listed them in his ''Early Science in Oxford, Vol. 2: Astronomy'' as "not extant".<ref>Gunther, R. T. (1923). [https://books.google.com/books?id=Yp0eAQAAIAAJ Early Science in Oxford, Volume 2: Astronomy]&nbsp;(NB Unfortunately this is the only volume of the series not currently (2018) available on Archive.org).</ref> But in 1936 during the refurbishment of the university [[Radcliffe Observatory]], he was alerted by the Savilian professor of astronomy, [[H. H. Plaskett]], to a chance discovery of "certain old metal bars and plates behind some cases."  These turned out to be part of the missing Savilian collection, including a {{height|ft=6|in=9}} mural quadrant, and an astrolabe of [[Queen Elizabeth I of England|Queen Elizabeth I]] which Greaves took on his 1637-40 expedition to the Middle East. Gunther wrote two articles in ''[[The Observatory (journal)|The Observatory]]'' on his findings, one shorter preliminary report{{refn|{{cite journal|journal= The Observatory |title=1937: April 9 meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society |year=1937 |volume=60 |issue=756 |pages=130–131 |bibcode=1937Obs....60..117. |url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/seri/Obs../0060//0000130.000.html |access-date=30 March 2018}}&nbsp;(NB Also refers to Gunther's article "The Astrolabe of Queen Elizabeth".<ref>[https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/archaeologia/article/iithe-astrolabe-of-queen-elizabeth/708A011718C1D9CEA19F11D4034EA7EA  ''Archaeologia'', vol. 86 (1937)].</ref>) In the first report Gunther seems mystified as to why Nicholas Greaves (who had the living of [[Welwyn]], [[Hertfordshire]]) should have had the instruments engraved as a gift from himself: but he was probably unaware of the letters from John Greaves to Pococke mentioned above. Gunther felt it significant that the presentation of the instruments synchronised with the appointment of Christopher Wren to the Savilian chair. Wren didn't in fact get the chair until 1661. Gunther also originally thought that the date 1637 on the quadrant indicated that it had originally belonged to Bainbridge, and Greaves had inherited them: but this is the year when Greaves travelled to the Middle East. }} with a fuller appreciation a few months later.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=The Observatory |title=The First Observatory Instruments of the Savilian Professors at Oxford |author=Gunther, R. T. |year=1937 |volume=60 |issue=758 |pages=190–197 |bibcode=1937Obs....60..190G |url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/seri/Obs../0060//0000190.000.html |access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref>

The inscriptions on four of the instruments (including Elizabeth I's astrolabe)<ref>[https://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/astrolabe/catalogue/browseReport/Astrolabe_ID=259.html Inventory no. 42223], Museum of the History of Science, Oxford. Retrieved 30 March 2018.</ref> read:

:1659 Acad. Oxon. in usum praecipue Prof. Savilianorum:
:Ex dono Nic Greaves S.T.D.
:In memoriam Tho. Bainbridge M.D. Jo Greaves A.M.&nbsp;&nbsp;<!--There are two spaces in the original-->N. fra: olim Astronomiae Prof. Savil.<ref>
1659 University of Oxford for the particular use of the Savilian Professors<br />
The gift of Nicholas Greaves, Doctor of Sacred Theology<br />
In memory of Thomas Bainbridge M.D. [and] John Greaves [[Master of Arts|Artis Magister]]&nbsp;&nbsp;brother of Nicholas [i.e. Nicholae frater]: sometime Savilian Professor of Astronomy</ref>

Greaves' other, smaller astrolabe didn't surface until 1971, when it was discovered by Gunther's son A. E. Gunther at his mother's house. The cataloguer of the OMHS attributes this to an oversight on Gunther's part.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/astrolabe/catalogue/browseReport/Astrolabe_ID=120.html |title=Provenance Report: Astrolabe_ID=120 |website=Museum of the History of Science, Oxford |access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref> The inscription around the edge of the limb reads: '1659 . Acad. Oxon. Ex dono Nic Greaves. S.T.D.'  It doesn't appear in Gunther's 1932 magnum opus, ''Astrolabes of the World''.

==Works==

Besides his papers in the ''Philosophical Transactions'' of the [[Royal Society]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Philosophical Transactions search page |website=The Royal Society |url=http://rstl.royalsocietypublishing.org/search?submit=yes&andorexactfulltext=and&y=0&fulltext=Greaves&x=0&format=standard&hits=40&sortspec=relevance&submit=Go|access-date=30 March 2018}}</ref> the principal works of Greaves are:

* ''[[Pyramidographia]], or a Description of the Pyramids in Ægypt'' (1646)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pyramidographia, or, A description of the pyramids in Egypt {{!}} Echoes of Egypt {{!}} Yale Peabody Museum |url=https://echoesofegypt.peabody.yale.edu/overview/pyramidographia-or-description-pyramids-egypt |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=echoesofegypt.peabody.yale.edu}}</ref>
* ''[https://archive.org/details/discourseofroman00grea A Discourse on the Roman Foot and Denarius]'' (1647)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greaves |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/discourseofroman00grea |title=A discourse of the Roman foot, and Denarius: from whence, as from two principles, the measures, and weights, used by the ancients, may be deduced |date=1647 |publisher=London : Printed by M. F. for William Lee |others=University of California Libraries}}</ref>
These were reprinted (together with a biographical notice of the author) as part of
:* Greaves, John (1737) [https://archive.org/details/miscellaneouswo13unkngoog ''Miscellaneous works of Mr. John Greaves'' Vol. I] and [https://archive.org/details/miscellaneouswo00bircgoog Vol. II]. London: Published by Dr [[Thomas Birch]], printed by J. Hughes for J. Brindley and C. Corbett. This also contains a reprint of<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greaves |first=John |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000393762 |title=Miscellaneous works of Mr. John Greaves, professor of astronomy in the University of Oxford, ... . In two volumes |date=1737 |publisher=Printed by J. Hughs, for J. Brindley, [etc.] |location=London}}</ref>
:* Withers, Robert (ed. John Greaves) ''A Description of the Grand Signour’s Seraglio; or Turkish Emperours Court'' (1653) London: Printed for Jo. Ridley, at the Castle in Fleet-street by Ram-Alley.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bon |first=Ottaviano |date=1653 |title=A description of the grand signour's seraglio or Turkish emperours court |url=https://lib.ugent.be/catalog/eeb02:10585830 |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=lib.ugent.be}}</ref>

* ''[[Pyramidographia]]'' was translated into French and published in ''[https://archive.org/details/relationsdediver00thve Relations de divers voyages curieux, qui n'ont point esté publiees...]'' (1664) Paris: Jacques Langlois, imprimeur ordinaire du Roy, pp. i-xxv [pdf 20-52], including Greaves' detailed drawings of the pyramids and mummies.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greaves |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TUEGAAAAQAAJ&q=John+Greaves+Pyramidographia+was+translated+into+French+and+published+in+Relations+de+divers+voyages+curieux,+qui+n'ont+point+est%C3%A9+publiees...+(1664)+Paris:+Jacques+Langlois,+imprimeur+ordinaire+du+Roy,+pp.+i-xxv+%5Bpdf+20-52%5D,+including+Greaves |title=Pyramidographia |date=1737 |publisher=J. Hughs, near Lincoln's-Inn-Fields, For J. Brindley, Bookseller to his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, in New-Bond-Street; and C. Corbett, over-against St. Dunstan's Church, Fleet-street. |language=en}}</ref>
*''[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_AKPuMIaYCcsC Elementa linguae Persicae, authore Johanne Gravio: item anonymus Persa de siglis Arabum & Persarum astronomicis]'' (1649) (''Elements of the Persian language'')<ref>{{Cite web |title=Elementa linguae Persicae / authore Johanne Gravio : item Anonymus Persa de siglis Arabum & Persarum astronomicis. |url=https://wellcomecollection.org/works/kagtgmeh |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=Wellcome Collection |language=en}}</ref>

Translations into Latin:
*''Chorasmiae et Mawaralnahrae hoc est Regionum extra fluvium Oxum.'' (1650).<ref>A manuscript copy exists in the Silesian Digital Library, Poland. (Dowloadable PDF) {{cite web |title=Chorasmiae et Mawaralnahrae, etc. |website=Śląska Biblioteka Cyfrowa |url=https://sbc.org.pl/en/dlibra/publication/47747/edition/44373/chorasmiae-et-mawaralnahrae-hoc-est-regionum-extra-fluvium-oxum-descriptio-ex-tabulis-abulfedae-ismaelis-principis-hamah-londini-ci-i-cl-reverendissimo-praesuli-jacobo-usserio-archiepiscopo-armachano-pietate-doctrina-coelestis-que-animi-virtutibus-maxime-conspicuo-has-binas-abulfedae-tabulas-unam-chorasmiae-alteram-mawaralnahrae-summa-observantia-d-d-joannes-gravius-abu-l-fida-isma-il-ibn-ali?language=en |access-date=9 September 2024}}</ref> A description of [[Khwarezm]] and Mawarannahr ([[Transoxiana]]) translated from the Arabic MS of [[Abu'l-Fida]], with tables of latitude and longitude for the principal towns. Dedicated to [[Bishop Ussher]]. A copy is in [[Merton College Library]].{{sfn|Merton|1880|p=2}}
*''Abulfedae Peninsulam Arabum''. This is an edited translation of part of [[Abu'l-Fida]]'s ''History''.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/stream/StudiesInIntellectualHistory/Bsih047Russell-ThearabickInterestOfTheNaturalPhilosophersInSeventeenth-centuryEngland_djvu.txt |title=Studies in Intellectual History - Volumes 001-050 |language=English}}</ref>
*''Binae Tabulae Geographicae'', two tables of geographical latitudes and longitudes translated from the Persian of [[Nasir al-Din al-Tusi]] and [[Ulugh Beg]]{{sfn|Merton|1880|p=207}}

The above three works appeared in Hudson, John (1712): [https://books.google.com/books?id=fq0-AAAAcAAJ Geographiae Veteris Scriptores Graeci Minores] Vol. III, Oxon. (in Latin)
*''[https://www.e-rara.ch/doi/10.3931/e-rara-13048 Lemmata Archimedis, apud Graecos et Latinos iam pridem desiderata, e vetusto codice manuscripto Arabico]''. This is a translation of part of [[Nasir al-Din al-Tusi]]'s edition of the so-called ''Middle Books''.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Jan P. |last=Hogendijk |year=2008 |url=http://www.xs4all.nl/~nirmala/Tarikhelm1.pdf |title=Two Beautiful Geometrical Theorems by Abū Sahl Kūhī in a 17th Century Dutch Translation |journal=Tārīkh-e 'Elm: Iranian Journal for the History of Science |volume=6 |pages=1–36 |publisher=History of Science Institute of the University of Tehran |access-date=8 August 2011 }}{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Greaves' unpublished MS was revised and amended after his death by [[Samuel Foster]]:
* Foster, Samuel (1659). ''Miscellanea sive lucubrationes mathematicae''. London: printed by R. & W. Leybourn, published by John Twysden.<ref>{{Cite web |title=e-rara / Search Author, Collaborator = "Foster, Samuel" [1-19] |url=https://www.e-rara.ch/search?operation=searchRetrieve&query=dc.creator=%22Foster,%20Samuel%22%20and%20vl.domain=erara%20sortBy%20dc.title/asc |access-date=2025-03-06 |website=www.e-rara.ch}}</ref>

The following book may not be by John Greaves, although his name appears on the title-page. First printed (posthumously) in 1706 for G. Sawbridge, and again in 1727, with a second edition in 1745, it discusses Greaves' findings and measurements of the Roman foot and denarius.<ref>The 1745 edition appears to be by another hand, but it may be an editorial attempt to modernise the language of Greaves, who died in 1650.</ref>
* Greaves, John (1745) [1706]. ''[https://archive.org/details/originandantiqu00greagoog The origin and antiquity of our English weights and measures discover'd...]'' 2nd edition. London: Printed for W. Payne and W. Bathoe.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Greaves |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-origin-and-antiquity_greaves-john-professor_1745 |title=The origin and antiquity of our English weights and measures discover'd. By their near agreement with such standards that are now found in one of the Egyptian pyramids. ... 1745 |date=1745 |others=Internet Archive}}</ref>
